findings.reason: Checked. Temkin §4.1.4 (p. 121, the same in arXiv v2) defines universal P-resolvability by the existence of 'a P-alteration f : Y′ → Y such that Y′ is regular and Z′ = f⁻¹(Z) is an snc divisor'. By §4.1.2 an alteration is proper, surjective, maximally dominating and generically finite, not projective. Its source, Exposé X §3.3.3 (Travaux de Gabber, arXiv:1207.3648, p. 159), requires 'a surjective projective morphism f'. So §4.3.2, which obtains the first claim of Theorem 1.2.5 (a projective char(X)-alteration b) from Theorem 4.3.1(i), gives no projectivity with the definition as printed. The review's note derives projectivity from 4.3.1(ii), and the counterexample to that derivation holds. Take S = X = Spec of a regular two-dimensional excellent local ring (universally resolvable, Exposé X Remark 3.3.4), f = id, Z the closed point, a = b = f′ = id and W′ = Z′ = V(xy). These satisfy every conclusion of (ii), including Z′ = b⁻¹(Z) ∪ f′⁻¹(W′) and log smoothness, yet b⁻¹(Z) is a point. Medium is right. One adjustment to the fix: the new source issue should state the projective form of §4.1.4, as in Exposé X, and record that the step '(i) follows from (ii)' in the proof Temkin copies from Exposé X (proof of Theorem 3.5, p. 162) needs b⁻¹(Z) itself to be snc. The statement of (ii) does not give this, so the blueprint must take it from the construction behind (ii). It should not assert that the printed proof of 4.3.1(i) already delivers it.

Checked. In the separable case Theorem 4.2.1 promises 'a separable projective P-alteration', and Step 4 (p. 122) takes a from Theorem 3.3.6 (p. 120), which gives only a P-alteration. Its field K′ comes from Theorem 3.2.12 (p. 118), whose proof works inside a maximal P-extension K̄. When char K = p ∈ P, a P-closed field is perfect, so K̄ contains K^{1/p^∞} and the finite subextensions chosen may be inseparable. The separable case is what Theorem 4.3.1(iii) needs: the proof of Exposé X Theorem 3.5, which Temkin's proof copies, uses 'Y is universally separably l′-resolvable … hence we can take c″ to be separable' (p. 164). The repair is right. If K is separably P-closed, its perfection is P-closed, because Frobenius twists of irreducible separable polynomials stay irreducible and separable over the perfect field. Also G_K = G_{K^perf}, with the same inertia and wild inertia, so K is separably P-tame and 3.2.12 and 3.3.6 run with a maximal separable P-extension. An equivalent, shorter repair replaces K′ by its maximal separable subextension. 'Affects: the proof' is right, and medium is right.

Checked. The proof of Lemma 3.2.10 (p. 117, the same in arXiv v2) takes f from Chevalley's theorem [EGA IV 18.4.6(ii)] and later uses 'f(t) is the minimal polynomial of a over K', which that theorem does not give. The counterexample is valid. With K = L = Q, O_x = O_y = Z_(p), a = 0 and f = t(t − 1), f′(0) = −1 is a unit, but A = Z_(p)[t, f′(t)⁻¹]/(f) ≅ Z_(p) × Z_(p) → Q kills the idempotent t. The repair works. The minimal polynomial g of a lies in O_x[t] because O_x is integrally closed, and f = gh by Gauss's lemma. Since f′(a) = g′(a)h(a) is a unit, the argument runs with g. The lemma stands, so 'affects: nothing' is right. Low is right.

All three checked, and all three passages are also in arXiv v2.
- (a) §3.1.7 (p. 115) says p : Val_K(X) → Val_K 'is injective if and only if X is separated', and §3.1 allows non-dominant situations. For the affine line with doubled origin over F_p and the rational point t = 1, Val_{F_p}(X) is a single point, so p is injective although X is not separated. Only the 'if' holds.
- (b) The proof of Lemma 3.2.10 says 'By the first part of the theorem' for the lemma.
- (c) Step 10 (p. 123, page image checked) prints 'the composition … is log regular', where log smoothness of the composition (with (X̄, T̄) log regular) is meant, and '(X′, T′) → (X, S) is log smooth' for (S, W). T̄ is never defined.
The fix is right. Low is right.

Checked. Exposé X §3.3.3 begins 'Let X be a noetherian scheme and let l be a prime invertible on X', and Theorem 3.4 assumes S universally l′-resolvable. So l is invertible on S there, that is, char(S) ⊆ {l}′. E1's review reason ('the Sylow trick needed tameness only over X, so char(X) ⊆ {ℓ}′ sufficed there') misstates the source's hypothesis, and Temkin's version with char(X) ⊆ P is more general than its source. The fix is right. Low is right: it corrects the record, not the mathematics.

Crossref for 10.1016/j.jalgebra.2019.02.017 gives Cossart–Piltant, 'Resolution of singularities of arithmetical threefolds', J. Algebra 529 (2019) 268–535; arXiv 1412.0868 was last revised in January 2019. Temkin calls [CP14] a preprint (Remarks 1.2.3, 1.2.6), so 'unpublished at the time' is right as history, but the prerequisite should cite the published version. §4.3.2 uses 'S is universally resolvable by [CP14]', the embedded universal form, not bare desingularization, so the restatement is right. One adjustment: state the restated item with 'projective' only if the design job confirms that Cossart–Piltant's resolution is projective (compare /1, since §4.1.4 as printed does not require it); otherwise state universal resolvability exactly as §4.1.4 does. Low is right.

§2.2.5 (p. 104) reads 'the p′-torsion group G = |l^×|/|k^×|. In particular, [l : k] = [l̃ : k̃]·|G|', the quotient of value groups. The item's '|l^×/k^×|' reads as the quotient of multiplicative groups, which is infinite for any nontrivial l/k. The fix is right; the formula is for finite tame extensions of a henselian k. Low is right.
